newsitem.title: SAUDI ARABIA: New fire put out as pilgrims mark Moslem feast.
newsitem.headline: New fire put out as pilgrims mark Moslem feast.

text.p: As two million Moslems in Saudi Arabia on Thursday marked the end of a haj pilgrimage in which a blaze killed 343 people, officials said a new fire had broken out but was quickly extinguished.

The Saudi civil defence authority said the fire, which was put out in minutes, caused no damage at the encampment in Mena, the site of Tuesday's blaze 11 km (seven miles) from the Islamic holy city of Mecca, the official Saudi Press Agency (SPA) said.
Witnesses said Thursday's fire had been small and did not keep them from performing the final rituals of haj and celebrating Eid al-Adha, the Feast of Sacrifice.

Huge crowds performed early Eid prayers in unison at the Grand Mosque in Mecca. Others made their way back to Mena, where Saudi authorities had rebuilt most of the 70,000 tents gutted in Tuesday's blaze.

Moslems in seamless white robes hurled stones at three pillars symbolising the devil, while police helicopters kept watch. The stoning was the final ritual of haj, which reached its climax on Wednesday at Mount Arafat where the Prophet Mohammad gave his last sermon 14 centuries ago.
Officials on Thursday still struggled to identify the dead and track down the missing.

"Oh my God, it was horrible," said Egyptian pilgrim Ehab as he made his way back to the Mena tent site. "People were running everywhere, but they could not get away because everywhere they went they saw fire."

Hundreds of ambulances had ferried the dead and some 1,290 injured to 12 nearby hospitals. Witnesses said many victims burnt to death, others suffocated from the deadly fumes while some were crushed by a stampede as panic gripped the pilgrims. They said many of the victims were old and too weak to escape the fire.
Nazer Ahmed, a Pakistani in his 60s, was being treated at An-Noor hospital for burns on 85 percent of his body. His face is so scorched he cannot open his eyes.
Mahmoud Sami, a 50-year-old Egyptian confined to a hospital bed, said he was not only feeling the pain from the burns on his back, hands and face, but missed his lost wife Raga and his son.
"We were not in danger when the fire started. We tried to flee the scene, but we were caught in the middle of the fire," he said. "I don't know anything now about my wife and my son."
Many pilgrims said they were shuttling from hospital to hospital in search of family members and friends.
"My heart is bleeding. It's terrible," one man said.

The Eid sermon at the Grand Mosque did not mention Tuesday's fire. Thousands of worshippers shuffled shoulder-to-shoulder around the black, cube-shaped Kaaba at the centre of the mosque, Islam's holiest shrine.
Some pilgrims shaved their heads with bare blades, while others slaughtered sheep for Eid al-Adha, marked by a billion Moslems worldwide.
This year 500,000 sheep and 15,000 camels and cattle were being slaughtered, Saudi media said, adding that the meat would be distributed to the poor in 27 countries.

Pilgrims, carrying umbrellas to ward off the sun in the 38 Celsius (100 Fahrenheit) heat, had to step over empty plastic water bottles and soft-drink cans littering the roads. At the site of the fire, the ground was strewn with burnt-out buses, melted electric fans and blackened metal tent frames.

The official media did not give the nationalities of the dead but diplomats said most were from the Indian subcontinent. The fire also engulfed Iranian, Syrian, Lebanese, Egyptian, Sudanese, Yemeni and Moroccan sections of the encampment.
Embassies said they still had no final figures for their dead, adding that many bodies were charred beyond recognition.

"Saudi authorities said they will release the bodies of victims to the embassy after Eid...maybe early next week," an Indian embassy official told Reuters. "We will not know the exact figure until Saudi authorities inform us."

Tuesday's blaze was the latest tragedy to strike the pilgrimage to Mecca, which able-bodied Moslems are obliged to perform at least once if they can afford it. In 1990, 1,426 pilgrims were crushed in a stampede in a tunnel and in 1994, another 270 people died in a stampede.
Saudi authorities gave no cause for either of the fires, but diplomats and witnesses said the first blaze had been caused by exploding gas cylinders.
